issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' For a severe mugging-related PTSD profile, markedly fragmented recall and very easy verbal access to the trauma narrative are hard to reconcile as describing the same current memory presentation.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: The Memory node is internally incoherent for a severe mugging/robbery PTSD presentation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests low avoidance and relatively integrated, verbally accessible trauma memory, whereas simultaneously endorsing very vivid detailed recall and body-based painful reliving implies a highly sensory, distressing, poorly integrated trauma memory. This combination is possible in milder cases, but here it is hard to reconcile clinically within the same Memory profile. The Negative Appraisals items are coherent for robbery trauma, but the Memory selections do not fit cleanly with that node pattern or with the strong Negative Appraisals ↔ Memory linkage in the formulation.

issues.item: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
issues.explanation: This item is more characteristic of ongoing threat/safety behavior than of a pure negative appraisal. In this profile, Threat is not endorsed and all Threat-related edges are inactive, while the active formulation is specifically centered on a Memory ↔ Negative Appraisals loop. The mistrust items fit robbery-related appraisals, but 'Constant Vigilance' introduces a prominent current-threat theme that is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

vignette:
Arjun, a 32-year-old South Asian man, had always been a diligent worker. As a housekeeper in a bustling hotel, he took pride in ensuring that every room was immaculate for guests. However, his life took a harrowing turn one night as he was returning home from work. He had just stepped off the bus when he was approached by two men in a dimly lit alley. They demanded his belongings, and in the chaos, one of them struck him in the stomach. The pain was excruciating, a visceral agony that seemed to echo in his body long after the incident. He gave them his wallet, trembling not just from fear but from the sheer unpredictability of the world around him. That night, as he lay awake, the memory of the attack became a relentless specter; each time it returned, he felt the same physical pain in his gut, as if the trauma was etched into his very being. 

In the weeks that followed, Arjun found himself haunted by vivid recollections of the attack. The details were so clear that he could almost relive the moment—the glint of the knife, the harsh words of his assailants, and the suffocating realization that he was utterly vulnerable. Yet, when he attempted to describe the event to his wife, words failed him. Each time the vivid recollection flashed back into his mind, it left him feeling even more convinced that he was weak and vulnerable, leading him to believe that he would forever be at the mercy of others. He would start to explain but would often falter, feeling as if he were trapped in a fog that obscured his ability to articulate the fear that had gripped him. This struggle left him feeling isolated, as though he were carrying a burden that he could not share with anyone.

As the days turned into weeks, Arjun's perception of the world shifted dramatically. His belief that people were not what they seemed made the memories of the attack surge even more vividly; he began to think that these recollections were proof of the world’s inherent danger, reinforcing his negative view of those around him. He began to believe that people were not what they seemed; the kindness he had always experienced felt like a facade. This belief that people were untrustworthy made the memories of the attack surge even more vividly, as he felt they confirmed his fears and underscored his vulnerability in a world filled with danger. The conviction that he could not trust anyone kept bringing him back to the memories of the attack, as if each recollection was proof of his failure to see the danger lurking around him. This conviction that he could not trust anyone kept bringing him back to the memories of the attack, as if each recollection was proof of his failure to see the danger lurking around him. This belief was fueled by the intrusive memories that replayed the attack, each vivid recollection reinforcing his conviction that he had been blind to the dangers around him. The world outside his home now felt menacing, a dangerous place where anyone could turn into a threat. He started to avoid the alley where the mugging had occurred, taking longer routes to and from work, all the while feeling a knot of mistrust tighten within him. This wariness seeped into his relationships. Once open and friendly, he now found it difficult to engage with colleagues, convinced that they could not be trusted. Even small interactions felt fraught with danger, as though every person he encountered could harbor ill intentions.

Arjun's negative appraisals of people and the world around him began to reinforce his intrusive memories. The more he believed that he could not trust anyone, the more the memories of the attack plagued him. Each time he recalled the event, the belief that he was weak fed directly into the vividness of the flashbacks; he wasn’t just remembering the attack, he was reliving it with the added weight of his own perceived helplessness. After the image broke through again, he caught himself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me. That conviction deepened with each flashback, leading him to conclude that the attack was not just an isolated incident but a reflection of his own inadequacies, further entrenching his negative self-assessment. Each time the vivid recollection flashed back into his mind, it left him feeling even more convinced that he was weak and vulnerable, leading him to believe that he would forever be at the mercy of others. Whenever he felt the familiar knot of mistrust, memories of the mugging surged forth, reminding him of his vulnerability. He felt trapped in a cycle where his thoughts painted the world as an unsafe place, and those thoughts brought back the vivid memories of pain and helplessness. Each time he recalled the event, he would feel that same gut-wrenching pain, a physical manifestation of his emotional turmoil, leaving him feeling even more vulnerable and distrustful. In those moments, he would catch himself thinking that if he had been stronger or more aware, he could have avoided the attack entirely, reinforcing his belief that he was weak for allowing such a thing to happen. The intensity of these memories deepened his negative self-assessment, leading him to think that he was inherently weak for allowing such an event to occur.

Despite his efforts to regain a sense of normalcy, Arjun struggled to cope. He began withdrawing from social gatherings, fearing that he might encounter someone who reminded him of his attackers. His relationship with his wife began to feel strained; she didn’t understand why he had become so distant, and he couldn’t find the words to explain. Arjun felt increasingly isolated, as if he were living in a bubble of mistrust and fear that distanced him from those he loved. 

Finally, after months of suffering and feeling trapped in his own mind, Arjun decided to seek help. Sitting in the therapist’s office, he felt a mix of fear and hope. He was terrified that he might never feel safe again, that the world would always remain a perilous place. Yet, deep down, he longed for the ability to trust again—to share his life with his wife without the weight of his trauma pulling him down. Arjun hoped that, through this process, he could find a way to reclaim the life that had once been so vibrant, before the darkness of the mugging had seeped into every corner of his existence.
